video_title: Pain Ahead For Markets As Interest Rates To Rise "For Generations To Come" | Chris Whalen
gist: Banking analyst Chris Whalen argues the post-2008 low-rate era is over: the 10-year Treasury could hit 5.5-5.75% within a year, mortgage businesses must plan for 7-8% rates, and the Fed will eventually be forced to buy Treasuries, triggering a dollar/bond stampede. He is cutting cyclicals and financials (sold Schwab, shorting consumer lenders on rising credit costs from the Iran-war energy/food shock), adding energy, gold and silver, and sees gold returning as the chief reserve asset in a pre-WWI-style competing-fiat world.

themes.theme: Structural rate reset and Treasury yields

insights.claim: Chris Whalen expects the 10-year Treasury yield to keep rising, potentially to 5.5%-5.75% within the next year, and warns that a rally back to 4% is a head fake.
insights.speaker: Chris Whalen
insights.so_what: Avoid positioning for a big duration rally; buying long bonds for a return to 4% is a trade he views as a trap.
insights.quote: my sense is 10-year Treasury keeps going up. I think it could be, you know, five and a half, five and three/4ers in the next year

insights.claim: Whalen tells mortgage industry clients that rates are not going back to 5% and that they must learn to run their businesses with mortgage rates at 7-8%.
insights.speaker: Chris Whalen
insights.so_what: Mortgage originators, homebuilders and housing-volume-dependent businesses face a structurally higher-rate operating environment.
insights.quote: we're not going back to 5%. You have to learn to run your business at seven or eight.

insights.claim: Whalen argues that current Treasury yields are as low as they will probably be for generations, contradicting President Trump's complaint that rates are too high.
insights.speaker: Chris Whalen
insights.so_what: Long-horizon thesis: secular bear market in bonds; treat today's yields as a floor rather than a peak.
insights.quote: they are as low as we're going to see probably for generations to come

insights.claim: Whalen's mechanism for higher yields is that duration removed by years of Bernanke/Yellen/Powell quantitative easing is returning to the market: the Fed no longer buys mortgages and Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac no longer hold big mortgage portfolios.
insights.speaker: Chris Whalen
insights.so_what: Absence of price-insensitive buyers of duration (especially MBS) argues for wider mortgage spreads and higher term premium.
insights.quote: Well, we're getting that duration back now. The Fed's no longer a buyer of mortgages.

insights.claim: Whalen says that while the Fed can always control the short end via Fed funds, a change in the composition of Treasury holders means it would need to buy far more long-term securities than in COVID (when it bought ~$7 trillion) to push long rates down.
insights.speaker: Chris Whalen
insights.so_what: Expect curve steepening risk: Fed cuts may not translate into lower long yields.
insights.quote: the short end belongs to central banks, right? We we've known that for years. That hasn't changed.

insights.claim: Whalen notes that credit default swaps on the United States priced in euros are widening, a gauge he discussed with David Koto (auto-caption spelling) for measuring global investor concern about US fiscal credibility.
insights.speaker: Chris Whalen
insights.so_what: Watch euro-denominated US CDS spreads as an early warning indicator for US sovereign risk and Treasury demand.
insights.quote: You look at credit default swaps on the United States priced in Euro, the spread is widening.

insights.claim: Whalen observes that triple-B investment-grade spreads over Treasuries remain quite tight because of a continued shortage of quality paper, but expects spreads to widen a long way.
insights.speaker: Chris Whalen
insights.so_what: Credit spreads have significant room to widen; tight IG spreads offer poor compensation for risk.

insights.claim: Whalen says the bond market has been 'doing its own thing' since the Iran war started in the first quarter of the year, with the yield move driven by the market rather than the Fed.
insights.speaker: Chris Whalen
insights.so_what: Bond vigilante dynamics are already active; fiscal/geopolitical shocks rather than Fed policy are driving long rates.

insights.claim: Whalen recently sold his Schwab position at a nice gain and has put on short positions in a couple of consumer lenders, expecting credit costs to rise due to the Iran war, energy and food prices.
insights.speaker: Chris Whalen
insights.so_what: Concrete positioning: short consumer lenders, out of Schwab; consumer credit is his preferred short.
insights.quote: I got out of Schwab a couple weeks ago with a very nice gain. I actually put down some short positions on a couple of consumer lenders

insights.claim: After seven to eight quarters of falling credit expenses, Whalen expects credit costs at banks and non-banks to turn and go much higher, as stressed consumers put groceries on credit cards they cannot repay.
insights.speaker: Chris Whalen
insights.so_what: Expect rising provisions and charge-offs to hit earnings of card issuers and consumer finance companies.
insights.quote: We we've had seven quarters of falling credit costs. It they're going to turn around and go the other way.

insights.claim: Whalen says Bank of America and Schwab have not restructured their low-coupon, high-duration securities books and will show ugly unrealized-loss numbers in Q3 and Q4 as yields rise; not fatal, but costing shareholders billions.
insights.speaker: Chris Whalen
insights.so_what: Expect AOCI/unrealized loss headlines and earnings drag at BAC and SCHW in upcoming quarters.
insights.quote: If you sat down and calculated how much the shareholders of Schwab and Bank America have missed because management couldn't figure out duration, it's it it's billions and billions of dollars.

insights.claim: Whalen credits Citi, JPMorgan, American Express (one of his favorites) and other big banks with managing duration correctly because they recognized the Fed's COVID policy was temporary.
insights.speaker: Chris Whalen
insights.so_what: Relative-value view within banks: favor duration-disciplined franchises like AXP/JPM over BAC/SCHW.

insights.claim: Whalen explains that SVB failed because it held 40% of its balance sheet in MBS and kept buying as the Fed hiked, so extension risk stretched average life from about one year to 10-14 years; Signature and First Republic were more idiosyncratic contagion cases.
insights.speaker: Chris Whalen
insights.so_what: Framework for screening banks today: MBS concentration and extension risk drive hidden losses when rates rise.
insights.quote: Silicon Valley Bank had 40% of their balance sheet in mortgage back securities

insights.claim: Whalen notes that bank loan growth is modest except for the 'all other loans' category, which captures margin lending and loans to hedge funds and private equity.
insights.speaker: Chris Whalen
insights.so_what: Bank loan growth is concentrated in leverage to financial players, a vulnerability if markets turn.

insights.claim: Whalen is cautious on all financials, including non-banks, mortgage companies and fintech, because many structures built during the ultra-low-rate COVID period are not sustainable at current rates.
insights.speaker: Chris Whalen
insights.so_what: Underweight the financial sector broadly, including fintech and mortgage non-banks.

insights.claim: Whalen argues last year's Wall Street boom and the stock rally of the past 24 months were primarily driven by Fed rate cuts (three in 2024 and three in 2025), and with that over the tailwind for financials is gone.
insights.speaker: Chris Whalen
insights.so_what: If Fed easing was the main equity catalyst, its end removes support for both financials and broad equity valuations.
insights.quote: The Fed was the catalyst for stock prices over the last 24 months. I think it's impossible to look at it any other way.

themes.theme: Fed under Warsh and fiscal dominance

insights.claim: Whalen views new Fed chair Kevin Warsh as a hawkish conservative who will try to be less interventionist and may lecture Congress about the deficit, especially after the midterms when Trump's lame-duck period begins.
insights.speaker: Chris Whalen
insights.so_what: Expect a less market-friendly Fed reaction function in the near term and more public Fed pressure on fiscal policy.

insights.claim: Whalen believes that despite Warsh's hawkishness, $40 trillion of federal debt means the Fed will ultimately have to buy Treasury securities to support the Treasury, as it did when the bond market stopped functioning in March 2020.
insights.speaker: Chris Whalen
insights.so_what: Plan for an eventual pivot to Fed balance-sheet expansion (debasement) after a period of market stress.
insights.quote: I do think overall the Fed is going to end up having to buy securities to support the Treasury, and that's when things get really interesting.

insights.claim: Whalen expects the path to forced Fed buying to be painful and to cause a stampede out of the dollar and Treasuries, which would become the catalyst for Bessent and Warsh to pressure Congress on spending.
insights.speaker: Chris Whalen
insights.so_what: A bond/dollar sell-off episode is the likely trigger for fiscal reform; hedge with non-dollar real assets.
insights.quote: it's also going to cause a bit of a stampede out of the dollar and out of treasuries and the bond market

insights.claim: Whalen states that whenever the Fed buys Treasury securities, bank deposits necessarily grow, a mechanical relationship that means large deficits imply more dollars created.
insights.speaker: Chris Whalen
insights.so_what: Fed monetization directly expands money supply, supporting the gold/debasement thesis.
insights.quote: When the Fed buys Treasury securities, of necessity, bank deposits grow

insights.claim: Whalen contends that if the Treasury slowed debt issuance, cutting the deficit in half each year, long rates would fall, because the dominant demand for Treasuries is as risk-free collateral for trade finance and currency swaps, not from end investors.
insights.speaker: Chris Whalen
insights.so_what: Fiscal consolidation would be bullish for bonds and stocks; supply, not investor sentiment, is the key yield driver.
insights.quote: The biggest demand in the world for US Treasury collateral is from trade and finance.

insights.claim: Whalen says stocks would soar if Congress credibly committed to fiscal consolidation, even including tax increases such as reversing the Trump tax cuts.
insights.speaker: Chris Whalen
insights.so_what: Austerity headlines may be a buy signal for equities and bonds rather than a sell signal.
insights.quote: and stocks would sore by the way if we do

insights.claim: Whalen believes debt-driven deficits now deliver much less GDP boost than in past decades, with the fiscal multiplier diminishing greatly.
insights.speaker: Chris Whalen
insights.so_what: A $2 trillion deficit is buying little growth, weakening the argument that fiscal stimulus supports earnings.

themes.theme: Iran war energy, refining and food shock

insights.claim: Citing energy analyst John Daart (auto-caption spelling), a former FT columnist, Whalen says about 30-35% of total global refining capacity in Russia and the Persian Gulf has been destroyed and will take years to repair, keeping energy prices high and causing demand destruction, e.g. in diesel.
insights.speaker: Chris Whalen
insights.so_what: Refining scarcity supports refiners and energy producers and keeps fuel-driven inflation elevated.
insights.quote: we have to repair all of the refining capacity in Russia, the Persian Gulf that's been destroyed, which is 30 35% of total global capacity

insights.claim: Whalen predicts a one-third global decrease in fertilizer use next year as farmers cannot afford diesel and fertilizer and producers shut down production, leading to lower crop yields.
insights.speaker: Chris Whalen
insights.so_what: Watch for a grain/food price spike in 2027; ag commodities and food inflation risk is underpriced.
insights.quote: We're going to see a onethird decrease in the use of fertilizer next year. That means yields are going to fall.

insights.claim: Whalen says the energy/food shock is baked in: even with immediate peace and free passage through the Strait of Hormuz, rebuilding refineries, gas production and supplies of sulfur and helium will take a couple of years.
insights.speaker: Chris Whalen
insights.so_what: A peace deal would not quickly normalize energy/industrial input prices; don't fade energy on ceasefire headlines.
insights.quote: And it's baked into the cake. There is nothing we can do about this.

insights.claim: Whalen expects inflation to raise prices for everything over the next 6 to 12 months.
insights.speaker: Chris Whalen
insights.so_what: Near-term inflation re-acceleration supports higher yields and real assets.
insights.quote: It's going to raise prices for everything in the next 6 to 12 months.

insights.claim: Whalen highlights specialized shortages, such as Group III high-end lubricants needed for high-efficiency engines, as an example of how the just-in-time petrochemical system breaks under disruption.
insights.speaker: Chris Whalen
insights.so_what: Second-order bottlenecks in specialty refined products may create pricing power for niche producers.

insights.claim: Whalen notes there are no refineries left in the western United States supplying adequately, California imports diesel and gasoline from Asia, and refineries in California will have to be reopened.
insights.speaker: Chris Whalen
insights.so_what: West Coast fuel supply is acutely exposed; watch California refining policy and regional fuel spreads.
insights.quote: We're going to have to reopen those refineries in California.

insights.claim: Whalen warns Europe faces a winter without enough gas to heat homes, worsened by Red Sea disruptions preventing Saudi oil shipments, fueling political shifts such as AfD gains in Germany.
insights.speaker: Chris Whalen
insights.so_what: European energy and political risk premium likely to rise this winter.

insights.claim: Whalen expects years of restructuring toward national self-sufficiency in energy, refining and industrial capacity, plus a possibly cheaper dollar that makes the US economy cheaper in relative terms.
insights.speaker: Chris Whalen
insights.so_what: Reshoring/resilience capex and a weaker dollar favor domestic industrial and energy infrastructure.

insights.claim: Whalen thinks AI will turn out to be a bust for investors: commercial users will pay, but constant introduction of cheaper models will make monetization very difficult.
insights.speaker: Chris Whalen
insights.so_what: Skepticism toward AI capex returns; downside risk for AI-hyped equities if monetization disappoints.
insights.quote: The AI, I think, is going to turn out to be a bust.

insights.claim: Whalen cites a Bank for International Settlements paper describing AI as circular finance, with industry players lending money to one another.
insights.speaker: Chris Whalen
insights.so_what: Circular financing in AI raises credit risk for lenders to data centers and AI firms.

insights.claim: Whalen predicts the K-shaped economy will turn into an L over time as stressed consumers fall behind, making affordability the dominant political issue of 2027-28.
insights.speaker: Chris Whalen
insights.so_what: Consumer discretionary and lower-income-exposed lenders face deteriorating fundamentals; populist policy risk rises.
insights.quote: that K is going to turn into an L over time

insights.claim: Whalen believes the reckoning comes in years rather than decades: rising costs will push Treasury interest expense sharply higher and be reflected in stocks and the dollar before 2028; he now sees housing prices rising in supply-constrained blue states and only a mild reset in overbuilt red states.
insights.speaker: Chris Whalen
insights.so_what: Revised housing view: regional divergence rather than a broad 2028 crash; fiscal stress timeline is short.
insights.quote: I think years as opposed to decades.

insights.claim: Whalen argues that the progressive experiment is over and that whichever party governs faces an age of constraint; Democrats will need a credible fiscal agenda or be 'laughed out of the room.'
insights.speaker: Chris Whalen
insights.so_what: Large new spending programs are likely to be punished by the bond market regardless of party.
insights.quote: we are going into an age of constraint and it doesn't matter which political party you come from

insights.claim: Whalen points to the rise of active ETFs as evidence that investors recognize passive index investing may not work as well going forward.
insights.speaker: Chris Whalen
insights.so_what: Supports shift to active, selective positioning versus passive index exposure.

insights.claim: Whalen has been reducing exposure to cyclicals and financials, increasing energy, and adding to gold and silver during this year's weakness, which he attributes mainly to rising interest rates.
insights.speaker: Chris Whalen
insights.so_what: Concrete allocation: long energy, gold, silver; underweight cyclicals and financials; use rate-driven gold dips to add.
insights.quote: decreasing my exposure to anything cyclical and anything financial and increasing my exposure to energy

insights.claim: Whalen keeps income in his portfolio and is a big owner of mortgage REIT Annaly, citing its well-managed, flexible management.
insights.speaker: Chris Whalen
insights.so_what: Annaly (NLY) is his named income holding despite his rising-rate view.

insights.claim: Whalen recommends a barbell: gold, real estate and real assets on one side and high-yielding assets on the other to pay bills in the fiat world, since all dollar-denominated assets are suspect.
insights.speaker: Chris Whalen
insights.so_what: Portfolio construction template: real assets plus high-yield income, avoid long-duration dollar assets.
insights.quote: So I think all dollar denominated assets are suspect. I'd like to have a barbell.

insights.claim: Whalen states global central banks continue to buy gold in volume, and that Russia delivered 100 tons of gold to China in the past year to help pay for the Ukraine war.
insights.speaker: Chris Whalen
insights.so_what: Official-sector demand remains a structural support for gold prices.
insights.quote: the Russians, for example, delivered 100 tons of gold to the Chinese in the past year

insights.claim: Whalen's long-term thesis is a return to a pre-WWI-like world where gold is the chief reserve asset and competing fiat currencies, including the dollar, are disciplined by their gold price; he says Bretton Woods is effectively dead.
insights.speaker: Chris Whalen
insights.so_what: Gold priced in each currency becomes the scorecard for fiscal credibility; long gold versus fiscally weak currencies.
insights.quote: The price of gold in the various currencies will be the discipline.

insights.claim: Whalen credits the Shanghai Gold Exchange as the catalyst for gold's return, providing a payment system outside the dollar/SWIFT network allowing settlement in yuan or gold, while China bans crypto but lets citizens buy as little as a gram of gold.
insights.speaker: Chris Whalen
insights.so_what: Non-dollar settlement infrastructure underpins sustained gold demand and gradual de-dollarization.

insights.claim: Whalen predicts gold will become a tier-one capital asset for banks and eligible collateral in currency swaps, potentially replacing Treasuries as swap collateral for oil payments.
insights.speaker: Chris Whalen
insights.so_what: Regulatory/collateral changes would add new structural gold demand and erode a key Treasury demand source.
insights.quote: You're going to see gold as a tier one asset for banks. They're going to be able to hold it as capital.

insights.claim: Whalen argues Bitcoin's fate is tied to the dollar because it has been co-opted by Wall Street, and it has no safe-haven value until it correlates positively with gold.
insights.speaker: Chris Whalen
insights.so_what: Do not treat Bitcoin as a debasement hedge; watch BTC-gold correlation as his test.
insights.quote: So until we see Bitcoin correlate positively with gold, it has no value as a as a a protection or as a safe haven for investors.

insights.claim: Whalen views Judy Shelton's gold-backed bond focus as on target but says issuing less debt overall matters more; he favors legislation declaring gold money rather than property and Treasury-issued weight-based gold coins.
insights.speaker: Chris Whalen
insights.so_what: Shelton's advisory role to Bessent is a watch item for any US policy move toward gold in the monetary system.

insights.claim: Whalen is developing a concept for gold-linked annuities, which he expects to gain traction with everyday investors seeking retirement security that holds value.
insights.speaker: Chris Whalen
insights.so_what: Potential new product category channeling retail retirement money into gold.
